questions.question: How do you implement a thread-safe Singleton in Java? Compare Double-Checked Locking (DCL) and enum-based approaches.
questions.title: Singleton Pattern — Thread-Safe Implementations (DCL vs Enum)
questions.direct_answer: Use the enum singleton for simplicity and safety, or the initialization-on-demand holder idiom for lazy loading. DCL with volatile works but is more error-prone. Enum singletons handle serialization and reflection attacks automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java Memory Model, volatile semantics, and class-loading guarantees
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting volatile on the instance field in DCL, or not knowing that enum handles serialization for free
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring @Component beans are singletons by default, making manual Singleton implementation rarely necessary in modern apps

sections.title: The Challenge Isn't the Pattern — It's the Memory Model
sections.content:
The Singleton pattern itself is trivial — a private constructor and a static accessor. What makes it an interview staple isn't the intent (one instance) but the implementation challenge: **making it thread-safe without destroying performance**.

A synchronized `getInstance()` method works but serializes every call through a single lock, even long after initialization is complete. In a high-throughput service calling `getInstance()` millions of times, that lock becomes a bottleneck for no reason.

Three approaches have survived scrutiny. Double-Checked Locking with `volatile` minimizes synchronization to the first call. The initialization-on-demand holder idiom leverages the JVM's class-loading guarantees for zero-overhead lazy loading. The enum singleton, recommended by Joshua Bloch in Effective Java, provides serialization and reflection safety for free.

The deeper question interviewers are probing is whether you understand the **Java Memory Model**. Without `volatile` in DCL, the JVM is free to reorder the construction of the instance — another thread can see a non-null reference to a half-constructed object. This bug is invisible in testing, intermittent in staging, and catastrophic in production. Understanding why `volatile` fixes it is what separates a memorized answer from genuine understanding.

sections.title: Three Thread-Safe Approaches Compared
sections.content:
| Aspect | DCL with volatile | Holder Idiom | Enum Singleton |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thread-safe | ✅ requires volatile | ✅ JVM class-loading guarantee | ✅ JVM enum guarantee |
| Lazy initialization | ✅ | ✅ (class loaded on first access) | ❌ eager (loaded when enum class loads) |
| Serialization-safe | ❌ needs readResolve() | ❌ needs readResolve() | ✅ automatic |
| Reflection-proof | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ (Constructor.newInstance throws) |
| Can extend a class | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ (enums extend Enum) |
| Boilerplate | High (volatile + synchronized) | Medium | Minimal |
| Recommended for | Lazy init + inheritance need | General lazy singleton | New code (Effective Java Item 3) |

sections.title: Why volatile Is Non-Negotiable in Double-Checked Locking
Holder Idiom and Enum: Simpler Approaches That Sidestep the Complexity
Key Points
sections.content:
- **volatile in DCL is non-negotiable** — without it, the JVM can reorder the constructor writes after the reference assignment, exposing a half-constructed object to other threads
- **Holder idiom uses JVM class-loading atomicity** — the inner class is loaded lazily on first access with zero synchronization overhead; my default choice when enum won't work
- **Enum singleton handles serialization and reflection automatically** — `Constructor.newInstance()` throws for enums, deserialization returns the existing constant; Effective Java Item 3 recommends it
- **Spring beans are singletons by default** — `@Scope("singleton")` is implicit, so manual Singleton implementation is rarely needed in Spring applications
- **Synchronized-method approach** works but adds a lock on EVERY `getInstance()` call, even after initialization — avoid it in any performance-sensitive code

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The challenge with Singleton in Java isn't the pattern itself — it's making it **thread-safe without killing performance**. Three approaches work correctly, and they differ in laziness, complexity, and resilience to serialization attacks.

**Double-Checked Locking** uses a `volatile` instance field with two null checks — one outside and one inside the synchronized block. The `volatile` keyword is mandatory because `new Singleton()` involves multiple writes internally, and without it the JVM can reorder the reference assignment before the constructor completes. Another thread sees a non-null reference pointing to a half-constructed object — fields still at default values.

The **holder idiom** is cleaner. A private static inner class holds the instance, and because the JVM guarantees class initialization is atomic and lazy, the first call to `getInstance()` triggers class loading which safely creates the instance. No `volatile`, no `synchronized`, no overhead after initialization.

The **enum singleton** is what Joshua Bloch recommends in Effective Java. The JVM guarantees one instance per enum constant, handles serialization automatically, and blocks reflection attacks by throwing on `Constructor.newInstance()`. The tradeoff is that enums can't extend a class.

In practice, most Spring applications never need any of this. `@Component` beans are singletons by default — the container handles lifecycle and thread safety. I only implement Singleton manually for pre-container utilities like connection pools or configuration caches that initialize before Spring starts.

questions.question: What is the difference between Factory Method and Abstract Factory patterns? When should you use each?
questions.title: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Factory Method lets a subclass decide which object to create (single product, one abstraction level). Abstract Factory creates families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes (multiple related products). Use Factory Method for one product hierarchy; use Abstract Factory when you need consistent families of products.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to distinguish creational patterns and select the right level of abstraction
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as interchangeable or thinking Abstract Factory is just a 'bigger' Factory Method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world example like UI toolkit families (Button/Checkbox per OS) for Abstract Factory, and Spring's FactoryBean for Factory Method

sections.title: One Product vs a Family — And Why Picking the Wrong One Costs You
sections.content:
Both Factory Method and Abstract Factory solve the same root problem: **decoupling the code that uses objects from the code that creates them**. But they solve it at fundamentally different scales, and choosing the wrong one creates either insufficient abstraction or unnecessary complexity.

Factory Method uses **inheritance**. A base class defines a method that subclasses override to return a specific concrete type. The framework calls the method, and the subclass decides what gets created. You're dealing with one product type — one thing that varies.

Abstract Factory uses **composition**. An interface declares creation methods for an entire family of related products, and concrete factories implement the complete family. The critical property is **consistency** — a `StripeFactory` produces a `StripeGateway`, a `StripeWebhookHandler`, and a `StripeRefundProcessor`, and you can't accidentally mix a Stripe gateway with a PayPal webhook handler.

The confusion interviewers exploit is treating Abstract Factory as just a 'bigger Factory Method.' The difference is structural: Factory Method relies on a class hierarchy (subclassing), Abstract Factory relies on object composition (delegation to a factory interface). Getting this distinction right signals that you understand the patterns at a design level, not just from reading summaries.

sections.title: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory Side-by-Side
sections.content:
| Aspect | Factory Method | Abstract Factory |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | One product type | Family of related products |
| Mechanism | Subclass overrides a method | Client delegates to factory interface |
| Extensibility | New product variant = new subclass | New family = new factory implementation |
| Consistency guarantee | ❌ (only one product) | ✅ (all products from same factory match) |
| Coupling | Inheritance-based (parent ↔ child) | Interface-based (client ↔ factory) |
| Spring example | `FactoryBean<T>` | `BeanFactory` / `ApplicationContext` |
| GoF intent | 'Let subclasses decide' | 'Ensure product family consistency' |
| When to use | Single hierarchy with variants | Multiple related products that must match |

sections.title: Factory Method: A Single Override That Controls Instantiation
Abstract Factory: Preventing Incompatible Product Combinations
Start Simple and Promote When the Pattern Earns Its Weight
sections.content:
**Factory Method first.** If you have one product type with multiple variants — notifications, parsers, validators — Factory Method is sufficient. The class hierarchy is simple, and the pattern adds minimal abstraction.

**Promote to Abstract Factory** when you need to enforce consistency across multiple related products. The signal is: 'If I create a StripeGateway, I must also create a StripeWebhookHandler and a StripeRefundProcessor, and they must all be from the same provider.' That consistency requirement is what Abstract Factory guarantees.

**Don't over-engineer.** If you have one product and two variants, a simple factory method (or even a `switch` in a static method) is cleaner than a full Abstract Factory with interfaces and concrete implementations. The GoF patterns have a cost — use them when the complexity they prevent exceeds the complexity they add.

In Spring Boot, `ApplicationContext` itself functions as a large Abstract Factory — it produces beans, events, resources, and environment properties as a coherent family. Recognizing this helps you see that you're already consuming Abstract Factory patterns daily, even when you're not explicitly implementing one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Factory Method = one product, inheritance** — a subclass overrides a creation method to return a concrete type; the base class owns the algorithm that uses the product
- **Abstract Factory = product family, composition** — a factory interface produces multiple related objects that must be used together; mixing products from different families causes runtime failures
- **Promotion signal** — when you catch yourself creating multiple related objects that must come from the same 'family,' upgrade from Factory Method to Abstract Factory
- **Spring's FactoryBean<T>** is Factory Method — override `getObject()` to control bean creation; `ApplicationContext` is Abstract Factory — producing beans, resources, and events as a coherent set
- **Adding a new product to Abstract Factory** requires updating the interface and all existing factories — this is the well-known trade-off vs adding new families (which requires only a new factory class)

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The core distinction is scale. **Factory Method** handles one product type with multiple variants — a base class defines a `createNotification()` method, and subclasses override it to return an `EmailNotification` or `PushNotification`. The mechanism is inheritance: the subclass controls instantiation, the base class owns the algorithm.

**Abstract Factory** handles families of related products. A `PaymentFactory` interface declares `createGateway()`, `createWebhookHandler()`, and `createRefundProcessor()`. A `StripeFactory` implements all three, guaranteeing every product is Stripe-compatible. The mechanism is composition — the client holds a factory reference and delegates to it.

The critical value of Abstract Factory is **consistency enforcement**. Without it, nothing prevents a developer from wiring a `StripeGateway` with a `PayPalWebhookHandler`, which would fail at runtime. The factory ensures all products in the family come from the same source.

My practical rule: start with Factory Method when you have one varying product. Promote to Abstract Factory when two conditions appear — multiple related products that vary together, and incompatible combinations that need prevention. In Spring, `FactoryBean<T>` is Factory Method — override `getObject()`. The `ApplicationContext` itself is a large Abstract Factory, producing beans, resources, and events as a coherent family. Don't reach for Abstract Factory if you have one product and two variants — that's over-engineering a solved problem.

questions.question: Explain the Builder pattern in Java. How do you design a fluent API with it?
questions.title: Builder Pattern in Java — Fluent API Design
questions.direct_answer: The Builder pattern constructs complex objects step by step, separating construction from representation. A fluent API returns 'this' from each setter, enabling method chaining. Lombok's @Builder automates boilerplate. Use it when a constructor would need 4+ parameters or when some fields are optional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of telescoping constructor problem and practical fluent API design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to validate state in the build() method, or exposing a mutable Builder to multiple threads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Lombok @Builder, the staged builder pattern for compile-time required field enforcement, and how Java record builders work in modern codebases

sections.title: When Constructors Stop Scaling: The 8-Parameter Readability Crisis
sections.content:
Imagine a constructor with 8 parameters: `new HttpRequest("POST", url, headers, body, timeout, retryCount, followRedirects, auth)`. Three months later, nobody remembers what the `true` at position 7 means. Worse, swapping two `String` parameters compiles silently but produces a bug that only surfaces in production.

The **telescoping constructor** anti-pattern tries to solve this with overloads — a 2-param constructor, a 3-param, a 4-param — each delegating to the next. But with 8 parameters where 5 are optional, you'd need dozens of overloads to cover every combination.

The Builder pattern eliminates both problems. A separate builder object collects parameters through **named methods** (`header("Content-Type", "application/json")`), applies defaults for omitted values, validates cross-field constraints in a single `build()` method, and produces an **immutable** result. Returning `this` from each setter creates the fluent API style that makes builder calls read like a specification rather than a constructor invocation.

In modern Java, Lombok's `@Builder` generates the entire boilerplate at compile time. But understanding how builders work manually is essential for designing APIs where the generated version isn't sufficient — staged builders, conditional validation, and complex defaults.

sections.title: Separate Required Fields from Optional Defaults
Validate in build() and Defend Immutability with Copies
Lombok @Builder and the Staged Builder for Compile-Time Safety
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Required fields in builder constructor, optional as setters** — callers can't forget required parameters; optional ones have sensible defaults and fluent setters
- **Validate in build(), not in individual setters** — cross-field constraints like 'POST requires body' can only be checked when all fields are configured
- **Defensive copies in the target constructor** — `Collections.unmodifiableMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(builder.headers))` prevents post-build mutation through the original builder reference
- **Lombok @Builder** generates the entire pattern at compile time — combine with `@Value` for immutable targets, `@Singular` for collection fields, `@Builder.Default` for defaults
- **Staged builder** provides compile-time enforcement of required fields through sequential interfaces — heavier than Lombok but prevents incomplete construction entirely

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Builder pattern solves the telescoping constructor problem. When a class has 6-8 parameters — some required, many optional — constructors become unreadable. Nobody remembers what the `true` at position 7 means, and swapping two `String` parameters compiles fine but breaks at runtime.

A builder separates construction from the constructor. You call named methods like `.header("Content-Type", "application/json")` that each configure one aspect and return the builder for chaining. The final `build()` call validates cross-field constraints and produces an **immutable** object.

The key design decision is **required vs optional fields**. Required fields should be constructor parameters of the builder — `Builder(method, url)` — so callers can't forget them. Optional fields are chainable setters with sensible defaults. Validation — like 'POST requires a body' — belongs in `build()`, not scattered across individual setters.

In modern Java, **Lombok `@Builder`** eliminates the boilerplate entirely. Combine it with `@Value` for immutable targets. The `@Singular` annotation generates accumulator methods for collections. For stricter compile-time safety, the staged builder pattern uses one interface per required step — you literally can't call `build()` until all required fields are set.

The pattern shows up everywhere in Spring: `UriComponentsBuilder`, `MockMvcRequestBuilders`, `WebClient` fluent API. Understanding the manual implementation helps when Lombok's generated builder isn't flexible enough.
